title: What C is and how a program is organised
goal: Distinguish source text, an instruction and an observable result. Edit a program to print a new sign on exactly two lines.

prerequisites.text: You only need to read short text. No previous C++ or other programming experience is required.

terms.title: Source code
terms.definition: The text you edit before building.

terms.title: Function
terms.definition: A named block of actions. In this environment the program starts at main.

terms.title: Standard output (stdout)
terms.definition: Where the program sends ordinary text. Code Studio shows it in the result area.

sections.title: From a sign to instructions
paragraphs: A workshop desk needs a sign with two lines: whether the workshop is open and which desk is free. A person can understand the request in conversation. A program performs the written actions and guesses neither the layout nor the colour of the sign.
C is a language for writing actions and calculations. This program does not sense the door or know its real state. It prints exactly the text between quotation marks.

Keep the file as main.c in Code Studio. The .c extension helps the environment select the language. C17 names the rules used by this course. Output you see after a run comes from the last successful build and execution.

sections.title: Two lines in execution order
paragraphs: Read the puts lines from top to bottom before running. Write the output without the quotes. What will a visitor read first?
steps: #include <stdio.h> makes the declaration of puts available so the compiler knows how to call it.
The block in main contains two calls to puts. Each action prints its text and ends the line.
return 0 signals successful completion to the environment. The zero does not appear in the output area.
trace: The first puts already ended its line

sections.title: Where to look when the result differs
paragraphs: If the number is wrong, find it in the quotation marks and edit just the digit. Run the file again. If the text stays the same, check the open file name and whether the run started.
The return 0 line does not print. Removing one puts changes the number of output lines. Editing a digit inside quotes leaves the number of lines unchanged.

sections.title: Use the same idea for a different sign
paragraphs: Your independent task is a sign for a loading dock. Retain the two-line structure, then decide on the new texts and where to put the additional action.
Compare standard output separately from exit status. Explaining which action printed each line is evidence of understanding in addition to matching the output.

reading.author: ISO/IEC JTC1/SC22/WG14
reading.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 — Programming languages — C
reading.purpose: Specifies how main starts in a hosted environment and how puts ends a line.

selfcheck.prompt: What does the worked program print?
options: Workshop open and Desk 2 on two lines
Both phrases on the same line
Workshop open, Desk 2 and 0 on three lines
feedback: Correct. Each puts ends its line.
Zero is the exit status, not standard output.

selfcheck.prompt: What should change to print Desk 7 on the second line?
options: Only the text in the second puts
feedback: Correct. Change the data for the second action.
The entry point name does not set the line text.
The number returned does not print.

selfcheck.prompt: Why would two lines of comments fail to replace the two printing commands?
selfcheck.feedback: Compare your explanation: an executed statement calls puts. A comment helps a human read the source, but does not create a printing action.

practice.title: A loading-dock sign
practice.task: Edit the starter. The first line must read Dock open and the second Bay 4. Preserve case, spaces and order. No input is needed.
criteria: stdout has exactly two lines in the requested order.
The source makes clear which action prints each line.
Changing Bay 4 to Bay 9 changes only the second line.
practice.hint: Find the one puts call. Fix its argument and add another puts immediately after it.

steps.action: Write down the two expected lines.
steps.why: You can compare a prediction with what happened.
steps.expected: Your prediction shows Dock open and Bay 4.

steps.action: Fix the text and add the second puts.
steps.expected: The run produces the two required lines.

steps.action: Check the result with a different bay number.
steps.why: This separates the data from the program structure.
steps.expected: Replacing 4 with 9 yields Dock open and Bay 9.

exercises.title: Transfer the idea
exercises.task: Use a separate copy. Keep Dock open, change the bay to 9, then swap the two commands. Predict the order before running.
criteria: The number and order change for different reasons.

teaching.scene: A workshop display takes plain text. A visitor should see two lines and know which desk is free. Trace the two commands and reconstruct their full output.

predict.prompt: What appears on the first and second lines when the sample calls run? How many lines does the result occupy?
predict.answer: The first puts writes Workshop open and adds a line break. The next call writes Desk 2 and adds its own line break. Two separate lines appear in call order.

apply.prompt: A different sign needs Stop 2 and Board now on separate lines. In which order would you issue the calls, and how would you check the result?
apply.answer: Write Stop 2 with the first call and Board now with the second. Expect exactly two lines with that case and the space between Stop and 2.

practice.strategy: Write the expected lines in order. Change one message at a time and compare each run with the corresponding expected line.
practice.diagnosis: If both messages are correct and Bay 4 comes first, inspect the call order. A merged line is a reason to check that both puts calls remain.

syntax.explanation: Standard output, stdout, receives program text. Each puts call writes the content inside the quotes followed by a line break.
syntax.mistake: Swapping the calls reverses the order of the displayed lines.
